newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU and EU enlargement poses unresolved issues.
newsitem.headline: EMU and EU enlargement poses unresolved issues.

text.p: Europe's single currency is likely to be the anchor for the countries of central and eastern Europe that want to join the EU, but monetary union is not seen as a barrier to the bloc's eastern expansion.

This is the view emerging among EU officials who say they are just beginning to grapple with how economic and monetary union (EMU) might affect the EU's greater political goal of opening membership beyond the current 15 nations.
Just how new EU entrants, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, would be linked to the planned single currency, the euro, would probably vary from country to country.

This is partly due to the different stages of economic readiness of the EU hopefuls and how near they are to matching the economic standards of the more developed EU members. Another factor is the way these countries manage their currencies.

Estonia and Lithuania, for example, have a currency board, a strict mechanism that pegs their currencies to the deutschemark and dollar, respectively. Latvia maintains a similar regime with the lat pegged to the International Monetary Fund's Special Drawing Rights (SDR).
The Czech Republic pegs its currency to the deutschemark, while Slovakia follows the dollar. Hungary has an adjustable peg to both the deutshemark and the dollar.
Poland, meanwhile, maintains a more eclectic approach with an adjustable peg for the zloty against the dollar, the mark the British pound, the French franc and the Swiss franc.
Romania and Slovenia have a so-called managed float for their currencies.
From a political standpoint, the EU is widely expected to begin taking in new members around 2002, well after the expected 1999 introduction of the euro.
The frontrunners are Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, with others following later.

Officials say there will be no compulsion for any new member to join a revamped European exchange rate mechanism. Dubbed ERM2 it is designed to provide a link between the euro and the currencies of EU members who are not among the first wave of EMU members in 1999.
In fact, there is strong reason to keep them out. One of the primary objectives of a future European Central Bank and the ERM2 is to maintain price stability in the euro zone.
This task is likely to prove difficult enough given that roughly half of the 15-nation EU bloc might not qualify for the common currency in 1999.

The inclusion of central European currencies would make keeping inflation under control much more difficult. A more likely scenario is for each new EU entrant to gradually find its way into the ERM2 and then eventually join the euro.
"Realistically, I think one can envisage a series of steps which allows the currencies greater stability against the euro," said one EU official.
Links between these currencies and the euro will depend on how rapidly and effectively they are able to meet broader economic convergence goals.
As with existing EU members, all newcomers will be subject to the EU's current procedure for preventing excessive budget deficits through a system of yearly evaluations.
However, the system that includes a maximum deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), will not be an additional hurdle for new EU members, officials say.

When a decision is made on which countries will be allowed to join the EU, the criteria used will be those drawn up four years ago in Copenhagen. These include requirements on democratic rule, the existence of a market economy, security, stability and good relations with neighbouring states.
Recent progress on the budget front among those most likely to join soon has been impressive. Hungary expects to have halved its 1995 deficit of 6.8 percent of GDP in 1996.
Poland is expected to bring its 1997 budget deficit below 3.0 percent of GDP -- one of the targets set by Maastrict Treaty for current EU members to join the single currency.
And while the outlook for the Czech Republic's finances has recently become less favourable, the budget deficit is still expected by analysts to fall well within the Maastricht Treaty's guidelines.
